mcq.q: At Mohan's request, Neel repairs Mohan's fence in March. In April, Mohan promises to pay Neel ₹2,000 for it. Is Neel's act good consideration?
options: No — past consideration is never valid
Yes — it was done at Mohan's desire, and past consideration is recognised under Section 2(d)
No — the promise came after the act, so it is a gift
Yes, but only if the promise is registered
mcq.explain: Section 2(d) recognises an act that "has been done" as consideration, so past consideration is valid in India, provided the act was done at the request of the promisor. Neel repaired the fence because Mohan asked him to, so Mohan's later promise to pay is supported by consideration and is enforceable.
mcq.fast: Ask two things: done at the promisor's request? Then past, present or future consideration all work.

mcq.q: Gita gifts her property to her daughter Mala on condition that Mala pays ₹10,000 a year to Gita's brother. Mala promises the brother in writing but then refuses to pay. The brother sues. He will:
options: Fail — he gave no consideration himself
Succeed — consideration may move from any other person, and Gita's gift is consideration for Mala's promise
Fail — he is a stranger to consideration and contract
Succeed only if he is a minor
mcq.explain: In India the consideration need not come from the promisee himself; Section 2(d) allows a third person to provide it. Here Gita's gift supports Mala's promise, and the brother may sue even though he himself gave nothing (Chinnaya v. Ramayya). Indian law, unlike English law, allows a stranger to consideration to sue.
mcq.topic: Legal rules — who gives it, and when
mcq.fast: Stranger to CONSIDERATION can sue in India; stranger to CONTRACT generally cannot.

mcq.q: Ashok agrees to sell his car worth ₹5,00,000 to Bhanu for ₹50,000. Ashok's consent was freely given. The agreement is:
options: Void for inadequate consideration
Voidable at Ashok's option
Void under Section 25
A valid contract — inadequacy of consideration does not invalidate an agreement freely made
mcq.explain: By Explanation 2 to Section 25, a low price alone does not destroy an agreement if consent was free. Inadequacy may only be taken into account by the court when deciding whether consent was free. With free consent proved, the contract stands.
mcq.topic: Legal rules — what qualifies as consideration
mcq.fast: Consideration need not be adequate — only real. Free consent + low price = valid.

mcq.q: Which agreement without consideration is valid under Section 25?
options: A written and registered promise made out of natural love and affection to a near relative
An oral promise to pay a debt that has become time-barred
A promise to pay for a service done at the request of a third person
A promise by a son to donate ₹1 lakh to a temple, made orally
mcq.explain: Section 25(1) protects a promise between near relatives made out of love and affection, provided it is written and registered. A time-barred debt promise is valid only if in writing and signed (Section 25(3)), so an oral one fails. The other two lack consideration and fit no exception.
mcq.topic: No consideration, no contract — and the Section 25 exceptions
mcq.fast: Section 25(1) needs ALL of: writing, registration, near relation, love and affection.

mcq.q: Deepak owed Esha ₹80,000; the debt became time-barred in 2024. In 2026 Deepak gives Esha a signed written promise to pay ₹50,000. Esha can recover:
options: Nil
mcq.explain: Section 25(3) makes valid a written promise, signed by the debtor or his agent, to pay wholly or in part a debt that the creditor could have enforced but for the law of limitation. The promise is enforceable to the extent promised — ₹50,000 here — not the whole original debt.
mcq.topic: No consideration, no contract — and the Section 25 exceptions
mcq.fast: Time-barred debt: written + signed promise -> recover only the amount PROMISED.

mcq.q: The rule that an outsider cannot enforce a contract made between two others is the doctrine of:
options: Caveat emptor
Privity of contract
Quantum meruit
Frustration
mcq.explain: Under the privity doctrine, an outsider to a contract has no right to enforce it, even if it was made for his benefit (Tweddle v. Atkinson). Exceptions include a beneficiary under a trust, family settlements, acknowledgement or estoppel, assignment and contracts through an agent.
mcq.topic: Suit by a third party — doctrine of privity of contract
mcq.fast: Who can SUE = privity. Caveat emptor is sale of goods; quantum meruit is a remedy.

mcq.q: Which person still CANNOT sue, i.e. is NOT covered by an exception to privity?
options: A beneficiary under a trust
A person entitled under a family settlement reduced to writing
A person to whom the promisor has acknowledged the payment
A person who merely expects to benefit from a contract between two friends
mcq.explain: Recognised exceptions to privity include beneficiaries under a trust or charge, persons entitled under a family arrangement, cases of acknowledgement or estoppel, assignment and agency. Merely expecting to benefit from someone else's contract creates no right to sue; that is the general rule, not an exception.
mcq.topic: Exceptions — when a stranger to the contract can sue
mcq.fast: "NOT an exception": pick the one with no trust, family, acknowledgement or assignment link.

mcq.q: Assertion (A): A promise to do what one is already legally bound to do is not good consideration.  Reason (R): What the promisee offers as consideration must go beyond what the law already obliges him to do.
options: A and R are both true; R does not explain A
A is true; R is false
A is false; R is true
A and R are both true; R explains A
mcq.explain: Both are true and R explains A. Performing an existing legal duty — for example, a witness under summons attending court — adds nothing new, so it cannot support a fresh promise. Consideration must be real and something beyond what the law already requires of the promisee.
mcq.topic: Legal rules — what qualifies as consideration
mcq.fast: R restates the rule that produces A -> option "R explains A".
